aspects.says: A closing delimiter on its own line ends the value with a newline; on the last content line it leaves none.
basis: section:The Closing Delimiter's Line Decides Whether the Value Ends With a Newline

aspects.says: A text block is a compile-time constant, the same pooled object as the equal literal, while a string built at run time is a separate object.
basis: section:A Text Block Is a Compile-Time Constant, the Same Object as the Equal Literal

aspects.says: A closing delimiter on the line after the opener gives the empty string, and one content line closed on that line equals the plain literal.
basis: section:The Opening Delimiter Ends Its Line, So Even One Line of Text Takes Two
aspects.reason: a test of the value cannot tell a text block from the equal plain literal, so there is no wrong solution to plant; the page shows the run

aspects.says: formatted() is String.format with the default locale, so machine-read text needs String.format with an explicit locale.
basis: section:formatted() Is String.format With the Default Locale, and Every % Is a Specifier

aspects.says: A text block joined with + to constants stays a constant and can be a case label; one with formatted() is computed at run time and cannot.
basis: section:A Text Block Is a Compile-Time Constant, the Same Object as the Equal Literal

aspects.says: lines() counts the same lines whether or not the value ends with a newline, while equals and a hash see the difference.
basis: section:The Closing Delimiter's Line Decides Whether the Value Ends With a Newline

aspects.says: Only white space may follow the opening delimiter before its line terminator; content or a comment on that line does not compile.
basis: section:The Opening Delimiter Ends Its Line, So Even One Line of Text Takes Two

aspects.says: Every % in a template starts a specifier, so a literal percent sign is %% and data goes in as an argument, never into the template.
basis: section:formatted() Is String.format With the Default Locale, and Every % Is a Specifier

aspects.says: Text read at run time gets none of javac's processing; stripIndent() and translateEscapes() apply the same steps.
basis: section:A Text Block Is a Compile-Time Constant, the Same Object as the Equal Literal
aspects.reason: the methods are practised in units 7.4.3 and 7.4.4, which own indentation and escapes; this page only names them
